title: Puppetserver

panels.title: JRubies Free
panels.description: Interpreters available to compile with, on the worst compiler. Zero means every incoming catalogue request is queueing, and it is what the JRuby exhaustion alert fires on.

panels.title: Waiting for a JRuby
panels.description: Mean time an agent request queues before it gets an interpreter. The alert warns above a second: past that, agent run times are visibly the pool rather than the work.

panels.title: Agents Turned Away
panels.description: The borrow queue hit its limit and agents got a 503. Not slow, refused: those runs did not happen at all.

panels.title: Borrow Timeouts
panels.description: Requests that waited for an interpreter and gave up. The same outcome as a 503 by a slower route.

panels.title: Catalogue Time
panels.description: Mean time to serve a catalogue request, queueing included. This is the number behind "puppet is slow", and the two sections below split it into waiting and working.

panels.title: Pool Size
panels.description: Interpreters configured per compiler. The denominator for the free count, and the thing you change when the answer turns out to be demand.

panels.title: Peak Pool Used
panels.description: The largest share of the JRuby pool in use at any moment in the selected range, across every compiler in scope. **This is a fraction of the pool and not a number of nodes**: average borrow time is not per-request compile cost, so nothing here converts to "how many more machines can I add" and a tile claiming otherwise would be guessing. Multiply it against your own growth. Amber near the top because at 100% the pool is fully borrowed and the next request queues, which is what Waiting for a JRuby beside this measures.

panels.title: Free and Requested JRubies
panels.description: Requested crossing above free is the moment agents start queueing. Requested pinned above free is a pool that is simply too small for the arrival rate.

panels.title: Agents Refused
panels.description: Runs that never happened, by how they were refused. Flat at zero is the answer you want, and the axis is floored so that reads as calm rather than as an empty panel.

panels.title: Queue Ceiling
panels.description: Configured max-queued-requests, the ceiling the refusals to the left are measured against. Above 150 it stops adding capacity: a request joining a queue that deep has usually timed out at the agent before an interpreter frees up, so the setting turns a fast rejection into a slow one and hides the shortage causing it. Read from the exporter host's own config, so on a multi-compiler estate this is the primary's setting.

panels.title: JRuby Borrow Rate
panels.description: Interpreters checked out per second, which is the compile rate this pool is actually serving. **The panels above say how much room is left; this says how hard it is being used.** Two free JRubies means something very different at ten borrows a minute than at a thousand.

panels.title: Wait Against Hold Time
panels.description: Wait is how long an agent queues for an interpreter; hold is how long it keeps one, which is the compile itself. Wait rising while hold stays flat means more agents arriving: add compilers or stagger the runs. Both rising means each compile got more expensive, and the section below says which part of it.

panels.title: Request Rate by Route: $host
panels.description: The demand side. Catalogue requests are the expensive ones; file_metadata volume is normal and cheap. A step change here with flat durations is the answer to this section.

panels.title: Route Duration: $host
panels.description: The service time side. The catalogue route dwarfing the rest is expected. The catalogue route climbing while the others hold steady is the code, not the server.

panels.title: Catalogue Phases
panels.description: The compile split into its own phases. Read this before the two panels beside it: they explain a number this panel establishes.

panels.title: Costliest Functions: $host
panels.description: The eight most expensive functions per compile. This is where an expensive custom function or a heavy hiera lookup shows itself by name.

panels.title: Costliest Resources: $host
panels.description: The eight most expensive classes and resources per compile, named. The most actionable panel on the board: it points at a file.

panels.title: Where Compile Time Actually Goes
panels.description: The ten profiled items burning the most time, ranked by mean cost times invocations rather than by mean alone. The panels above answer "what is slow when it runs"; this one answers "where did the time go", and they routinely disagree: something cheap called ten thousand times outranks something expensive called twice. **Approximate by construction** -- the mean is the lifetime mean rather than this window's, so read the ranking rather than the absolute seconds. Subject to the same Profiler Overflow caveat as the panels above.

panels.title: Calls Out: $host
panels.description: What Puppetserver waits on that is not its own work: PuppetDB queries and commands, and the classifier. If these are what grew, the problem is not here and the PDCTNG PuppetDB link at the top of this board carries your time range across.

panels.title: File Sync
panels.description: Code distribution to this compiler. PE only, so it renders empty on FOSS, which is honest. A clone taking seconds is normal after a deploy and abnormal at any other time.

panels.title: Profiler Overflow
panels.description: Profiler tables that filled up and stopped accepting new entries. Above zero, the costliest lists on this row are incomplete and should not be read as a ranking.

panels.title: Outbound Calls, By Volume
panels.description: Outbound calls per second by operation. **Calls Out above says which one is slow; this says which one we make constantly**, and they are rarely the same. A cheap call made ten thousand times costs more than an expensive one made twice, and only this panel can say so.

panels.title: Heap
panels.description: Used against max. The shape that matters is the sawtooth floor rising: each collection recovering less than the last, which is the classic out-of-memory precursor.

panels.title: GC Time Fraction
panels.description: Seconds of collection per second of life, per collector. A rising fraction is the JVM about to fall over, and it moves before the heap panel beside it does.

panels.title: CPU
panels.description: Share of the machine this process is using, and how much of that is garbage collection. A compiler pinned at the top of this panel cannot be fixed by adding JRubies to it.

panels.title: Threads
panels.description: Live threads against the peak this process has ever reached. Peak far above current is a burst that has already happened.

panels.title: File Descriptors Used
panels.description: Open descriptors as a share of the process limit. Exhaustion kills Puppetserver with symptoms that point everywhere except here.

panels.title: Non-Heap Memory
panels.description: Metaspace and code cache, the memory heap tuning does not touch. **A slow rise here with a flat heap is a classloader leak**, usually from environment churn, and it ends in an out-of-memory that looks nothing like a heap problem. `max` is excluded because metaspace is unbounded by default and reports -1.

panels.title: GC Runs, And The Last Pause
panels.description: Collections per second per collector, with the most recent pause each one took. **GC Time Fraction above cannot tell a hundred short pauses from one long one** and they need different fixes: frequent young collections are an allocation rate, a long old-generation pause is a heap being walked in full and is what times an agent out.

panels.title: Time To JRuby Pool Exhaustion

defaults.noValue: Nothing heading for the pool wall

panels.description: How long until this compiler has no free JRubies, at the rate they are being used up over the last forecast window. **Empty is the healthy state**: the series only exists while free JRubies are falling, so nothing to draw means nothing is heading for the wall. A line that appears and drops steeply is a fleet outgrowing its compilers. PdctngJrubyPoolExhaustionForecast pages when this falls under the configured threshold.

description: Can agents get a compiler, and if catalogues are slow, is it demand or the code. Requires enable_service_metrics on the exporter.
